source: Feher da Silva and Hare (2020) Humans primarily use model-based inference in the two-stage task (bioRxiv v1 full PDF; Nat Hum Behav 2020)
finding: Re-read of Table 1 closes gap 10. Hybrid weight w is much higher when instructions are a full story, and a purely model-based agent with a wrong task model gets labelled hybrid.
numbers: Median w (25th-75th pct): Daw 2011 N=17: 0.39 (0.29-0.59). Kool 2016 N=206: 0.24 (0.00-0.68). Spaceship N=21: 0.78 (0.61-0.91). Magic carpet N=24: 0.79 (0.51-0.85). Simulated purely model-based agents: 0.94 with correct task model (95% 0.74-1.00), 0.36 with 'unlucky symbol' wrong model (95% 0.24-0.48), 0.80 with TDLR wrong model. Posterior prob. that new-task mean w exceeds Kool 2016 mean > 0.9999. In Kool 2016 data 111 of 206 had configuration-mistake prob < 0.1 and 51 had higher mistake rates; median mistake prob 0.54 when symbols switched sides.
quote: more detailed task instructions lead participants to make primarily model-based choices that show little, if any, model-free influence
limits: All six numbers in the gap list confirmed (0.24, 0.39, 0.78, 0.79 observed; 0.94, 0.36 simulated). Read from the preprint v1 PDF; the Nature Human Behaviour page was only opened at abstract level. Samples are small (21 and 24) and tasks differ from the original.
agent_relevance: Low w in a planning-gate test may mean the agent misread the task, so give the agent a full task description before judging 'habit'.

source: Kool, Gershman and Cushman (2017) Cost-benefit arbitration between multiple reinforcement-learning systems, Experiment 1 (Psychol Sci 28:1321)
finding: Closes gap 4 in part. With extensive, step-by-step instructions and comprehension checks, people used more model-based control on high-stakes trials when model-based control paid off.
numbers: Exp 1: 101 recruited, 98 analysed. Mean w 0.76 on high-stakes vs 0.54 on low-stakes trials, t(97)=4.67, p<.001, d=0.47. Behavioural (regression) index of model-based choice also up, d=0.32. Stakes also raised inverse temperature, d=0.40. Footnote replication with negative reward range, N=93: w 0.62 vs 0.51, t(93)=2.81, p=.006, d=0.29.
limits: Instruction was extensive (25 practice trials, transitions and rewards taught one element at a time, no time limit) but it is not the Feher da Silva story format. Overall mean w stays well below 1 (0.40 to 0.65), so some mixing remains. Online workers; N about 100.
agent_relevance: Cost-benefit arbitration survives good instructions. Effect size is small to medium (d 0.29-0.47). A gate that raises planning when the payoff is higher has human precedent.

source: Kool, Gershman and Cushman (2017) Experiment 2 and between-experiment test
finding: In a task variant where model-based control gives no accuracy gain, raising stakes did not raise model-based control. This is the payoff-gap logic in a human sample.
numbers: Exp 2: N=100 analysed. Mean w 0.39 (high stakes) vs 0.41 (low), t(99)=-0.38, p=.71, d=-0.04. Behavioural model-based index: t(99)=-0.72, p=.470, d=-0.07. Inverse temperature still rose with stakes, d=0.40. Between experiments: stakes effect on w larger in Exp 1, t(196)=3.56, d=0.51; behavioural index t(196)=3.29, d=0.47; mean w 0.65 (Exp 1) vs 0.40 (Exp 2), t(196)=6.21, d=0.88.
limits: Null effect in Exp 2 rests on a modest N and one task design. Between-experiment comparison is not randomised assignment.
agent_relevance: Planning use should track the payoff gap, not stakes alone: the gate must estimate whether slow thinking would change the answer, not only how much the answer is worth.

source: Europe PMC abstract (PMID 41083652, 2026) When models matter: environmental demand guides the arbitration between model-based and model-free control
finding: A newer, larger human sample (n=140) shows people learn to regulate model-based use from how often it pays: more first-stage alternations gave more model-based test-phase choice than more repetitions.
numbers: n=140; two-stage-style task with deterministic first-stage mapping; between-group exposure manipulation. Effect size not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; authors and effect size not read. Different task from the Daw two-step.
agent_relevance: Supports learned, cost-benefit use of planning in a fresh sample. Evidence for a learned gate, not a fixed one.

source: Keramati, Smittenaar, Dolan and Dayan (2016) Adaptive integration of habits into depth-limited planning (PNAS 113:12868), PMC full text
finding: Gap 9 for Keramati 2016: design and key tests re-read. Time pressure is a between-group manipulation with 15 per group, so the sample was never large.
numbers: Three-step task, about 400 trials. High-resource group n=15, 2 s to respond; low-resource group n=15, 700 ms. Planning depth k=0 (habit), 1 (plan-until-habit), 2 (full plan). High-resource group: pure planning effect after rewarded and unrewarded trials, both P<0.001 (Wilcoxon). Plan-until-habit effect only after unrewarded trials, P<0.002; after rewarded trials P=0.073 (not significant).
limits: Replication: a scan of 137 records citing the paper (Europe PMC, 2026-10-31) found no direct same-design replication with larger groups. Related work uses different tasks (for example a 60-participant habit-goal task under time pressure, 2026, abstract only). Replication status stays open.
agent_relevance: Depth-limited planning with cached tail values has human support from one n=15 vs n=15 study. Treat as a design hint, not a settled law.

source: Otto, Gershman, Markman and Daw (2013) The curse of planning: dissecting multiple reinforcement-learning systems by taxing the central executive (Psychol Sci 24:751)
finding: Gap 9 for Otto 2013 (load, not stress). A concurrent numerical Stroop load removes the model-based signature on the follow-on choice, and model-based choices are slower.
numbers: Exp 1: 43 recruited, 25 analysed (within subject). Lag 2 mixing weight larger than Lag 0 and Lag 1 weights, t(24)=2.94, p<.01. Lag 2 x reward x transition interaction p<.05; Lag 0 and Lag 1 interactions ps>.25. Lag 2 first-stage RTs slower than Lag 1, p<.05. Exp 2 is a between-subjects replication with a tone-counting load (N not extracted).
limits: Small analysed samples; 18 of 43 excluded in Exp 1. No later large preregistered replication found in a 252-record citing scan. A tDCS study (n=22) found no effect on model-based control, but that is a different manipulation.
agent_relevance: Context load is a plausible reason to drop planning: keep slow-pass context clean when the gate needs it.

source: Citing-literature scan of Keramati 2016 and Otto 2013 plus nearby results (Europe PMC abstracts: PMIDs 24475185, 36701316, 41286251, 40206860)
finding: No larger direct replication of either study turned up. Neighbours: right DLPFC anodal tDCS (n=22, within subject) did not change model-based or model-free control (Bayes favours no effect); trait mind wandering relates to weaker model-based choice; two time-pressure habit paradigms (forced-response, outcome devaluation) replicate within themselves but do not correlate with each other; humans pick the minimum needed planning depth in problems needing 1 to 8 subgoals.
numbers: tDCS: 22 participants, power at least 60%. Habit measures: 4 days of training per paradigm, reliable measures, no convergent validity. Planning-depth study: depths 1 to 8 (2025).
limits: Abstract-level only. Different tasks; none is a replication of Keramati 2016 or Otto 2013.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code that load or time pressure always cuts planning; effects depend on the paradigm.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut and Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (arXiv 2410.05563 v3)
finding: Closest LLM study to an explicit value-of-computation rule. Reward = log P(answer | chain) - log P(answer | question) - lambda x tokens, used to train the model by expert iteration so it reasons only when worth it. It is a trained policy, not a gate tested against fixed and random routing at equal tokens.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B (base and instruct). Averaged over datasets, an 8B-class model: RaM accuracy 63.5% at 146.2 output tokens vs STaR 61.9% at 215.1 and few-shot CoT 56.4% at 253.6; a 3B-class model: RaM 50.1% at 170.8 vs STaR 47.4% at 222.7. Reported saving 23 to 45% fewer output tokens than CoT or STaR across three models. Hard vs easy chain length: RaM 139 vs 89 tokens (36.0% shorter on easy) against plain CoT prompting 228 vs 226 (0.9%). Out-of-distribution MMLU-CF: 28 to 36% fewer tokens than STaR.
limits: Small open-weight models; cost is output tokens; no random-routing or fixed-budget control and no cost-adjusted utility table. Savings smaller on reasoning-heavy tasks than on knowledge tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 only partly closed: a VOC reward works for training and chain length varies with difficulty, but no equal-token gate comparison exists here.

source: He and Feng (2026) When to Think Deeply: Inhibitory Deliberation for LLM Reasoning (arXiv 2606.06745), Table 1 re-read
finding: Best head-to-head of cheap signals on the same items and the closest test of a gain-minus-cost gate. A learned controller predicts quality gain and slow-token cost from fast-answer evidence; compared with random and confidence selection at the same slow-call count.
numbers: Held-out 5,000 math items (GSM8K plus Mixture-of-Thoughts), fast Qwen2.5-Math-7B, slow OpenR1-Distill-7B, slow rate 8.20% for all routed methods. Always-Fast 47.90% (utility 0.4789, 5.26 avg tokens). Random Same-k 46.76% (-1.14; utility 0.4517; 517.91 tokens; corrective precision 13.41). Low Avg LogProb Same-k 48.22% (+0.32; 0.4646; 582.68; 21.22). Low Logit Gap Same-k 47.84% (-0.06; 0.4571; 714.73; 11.46). IDPR learned gate 48.92% (+1.02; 0.4731; 519.42; 27.07).
limits: Equal slow-call count, not equal total tokens (518 to 715 average tokens). Cost-aware utility of every routed method is below Always-Fast (0.4789), so the gate does not pay on this metric. Gain is +1.02 points for about 514 extra tokens per item on average. Math only, one model pair. Verbalised confidence and sample disagreement were not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly closed: average log-prob beat logit gap (+0.32 vs -0.06) and both beat random; a learned gate beat both. Gap 1: a gain-minus-cost gate exists, but on cost-adjusted utility it lost to never thinking.

source: Yue et al. (2024) Large Language Model Cascades with Mixture of Thought Representations for Cost-efficient Reasoning (ICLR 2024; arXiv 2310.03094)
finding: Head-to-head of routing signals from a weak model to GPT-4 on the same items: sample agreement (vote) vs a GPT-3.5 verifier prompt vs fine-tuned RoBERTa verifiers. Answer consistency of the weak model's samples is the signal.
numbers: GSM8k (cost relative to GPT-4 = 1.0): GPT-3.5 CoT-SC acc 0.842 at cost 0.111; LLM-as-verifier on question (LLM-Q) 0.884 at 0.253; LLM-QA 0.862 at 0.135; Finetuned-Q 0.892 at 0.340; Finetuned-QA 0.882 at 0.262; MoT-1D-Vote threshold 0.5: 0.917 at 0.235; threshold 0.7: 0.951 at 0.425; MoT-Verify 0.947 at 0.401; GPT-4 CoT-SC 0.958 at 1.000. Abstract claim: comparable to GPT-4 at 40% of the cost. With Llama2-13B as weak model, GSM8k and CREPE showed no saving (accuracy and cost changed roughly linearly).
limits: Decision cost is counted for external verifiers; for votes the cost is the extra samples. Two proprietary models; 2023 price ratio about 30x. The gate fails when the weak model is too poor.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: sample disagreement beat verifier-style signals at equal or lower cost on GSM8k. Gap 3: a break-even exists only if the fast model is good enough.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: strategies for eliciting calibrated confidence from RLHF language models (EMNLP 2023; arXiv 2305.14975)
finding: Verbalised confidence vs token probability on the same items for gpt-3.5-turbo. Verbal is better calibrated and about equal or better for ranking. This predicts correctness of one answer, not whether a slow pass would change it.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, ECE / AUC. TriviaQA: label prob 0.140 / 0.869; verbalised 1-stage top-4 0.054 / 0.896. SciQ: label prob 0.256 / 0.752; verbalised top-2 0.132 / 0.766. TruthfulQA: label prob 0.451 / 0.418; verbalised top-1 0.389 / 0.545. Entropy AUC 0.547, 0.483, 0.236. Llama2-70B-Chat, TriviaQA: label prob ECE 0.151, AUC 0.865 vs verbalised top-4 0.069 / 0.816, so for that model token probability ranks better.
limits: Short-answer QA; 2023 models; target is correctness, not slow-pass benefit.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no single winner. Verbalised confidence is cheap and better calibrated for chat models; token probability can rank better for some open models.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for efficient reasoning and coding with LLMs (EMNLP 2023; arXiv 2305.11860)
finding: Sample agreement as a stopping rule: stop sampling when a Dirichlet-based test says the majority answer will hold. Saves samples with almost no accuracy loss. A cheap gate that uses disagreement as the uncertainty signal.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs. Up to 7.9 times fewer samples, average accuracy drop below 0.1%. Worked example: majority count 9 of the first 10 samples gives over 99% chance the majority holds after 40.
limits: Saves parallel samples, not reasoning depth; assumes an answer format that can be voted on.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 6: the gate's own cost is the samples already drawn, and savings are large when most items are easy.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: Closest measured break-even by difficulty. Test-time compute pays on easy and medium questions, much less on the hardest, and compute-optimal allocation by difficulty beats best-of-N.
numbers: MATH with PaLM 2-S: compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute. FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger model: test-time compute wins on easy and intermediate bins and when inference load is low (R=0.16); mixed at R=0.79; at R=22 pretraining wins; little gain on the hardest bin.
limits: Difficulty bins come from the model's own pass rate and need compute to estimate; the authors say difficulty estimation 'requires applying a non-trivial amount of test-time compute'. One task family and one model family; no token-price axis in the Kool sense.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: a break-even exists and depends on difficulty and inference load. Gap 6: gate (difficulty estimate) cost is real and unpriced.

source: Paglieri et al. (2025) Learning When to Plan (arXiv 2509.03581), Table 3 and appendices C.3, C.5
finding: Gap 7 and gap 3: the best planning frequency is not fixed. Goldilocks curves appear in all environments and models tried, but shapes differ and no rule predicts the peak. A token penalty cut planning frequency without hurting score after training.
numbers: Llama-3.3-70B zero-shot on Crafter (100 seeds): never plan reward 0.343 at 559.6 tokens; plan every 4 steps 0.379 at 11,510.9; always plan 0.349 at 38,836.2. SFT 8B: never 0.286 (991.5 tokens); dynamic 0.343 (1,869.9); SFT+RL dynamic 0.387 at 1,714 tokens. Llama-3.1-8B degrades sharply the more it plans. Gemini 2.5 Flash degrades with always-plan on Crafter and on POGS. TextWorld: planning gives only moderate gains. RL token penalties (-0.001 and -0.005 per token) reduced plan frequency and length with the score 'largely unaffected'. KL coefficient 0.1 is a sweet spot; 0.05 collapses planning frequency; 0.3 raises invalid actions.
limits: A zero-shot dynamic baseline is absent (authors could not elicit it by prompt). The every-4 optimum was found by sweep, not predicted. Reward gain of 0.036 costs about 11k tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: must be tuned per environment and model; the best rule seen is a token penalty plus RL. Gap 3: planning every step costs 3.4 times the tokens of every-4 for a lower score.

source: Liu, Wang, Wang, Guo and Li (2026) Imagine-then-Plan (arXiv 2601.08955), lookahead comparison and latency profile
finding: Adaptive lookahead (a trained predictor chooses imagination horizon) beats fixed-k and random-k on the success-versus-token-budget curve. Gives some gate cost data and a rule: longer-horizon tasks favour larger lookahead.
numbers: ALFWorld, Qwen3-8B policy and world model, 140 tasks in 14 folds, normalised token budget NB(k). Fixed-k success peaks at moderate k then declines while cost rises sharply. Adaptive reaches higher success at lower budget than fixed and than Random Lookahead. Compute-matched no-world-model baselines (Table 5): best prompting baseline K-candidate selection 36.42 vs ITP-I 41.43 (+5.01); best training baseline 78.14 vs ITP-R 88.57 (+10.43). Deployment profile: decision latency 14.2 s median per step (policy 5.1 s, imagination 7.8 s), p95 31.8 s.
limits: Predictor cost not separated from imagination cost. Fixed-k and random numbers are in figures only. Authors note higher inference-time overhead.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 7: adaptive beat random at a matched budget; horizon scales with task horizon. Gap 6: the gate head is small, imagination dominates cost.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage (NeurIPS 2023; arXiv 2305.17390), switch rule, Swift-only ablation, tokens per action
finding: Gap 6: the switch is a free rule (no tokens), the fast module is a small fine-tuned model, and the slow LLM runs only when needed. The Swift-only ablation shows how much the slow pass adds.
numbers: Switch to slow if: 5 steps of zero reward, invalid action, critical decision, or unexpected observation. Tokens per action: SwiftSage 757.07 vs SayCan 1,855.84, ReAct 1,971.03, Reflexion 2,983.46. ScienceWorld with gpt-3.5-turbo (Table 3, overall): Swift-only 49.22, SayCan 25.22, ReAct 19.76, Reflexion 23.40, SwiftSage 62.22 (slow pass adds +13.0 points; Swift-only already beats the ChatGPT baselines). Each SAGE call uses two LLM calls and yields about 5 actions.
limits: Fast module is fine-tuned on oracle trajectories, so its training cost is outside the token count. Baselines are not equal-compute. Authors list a trainable switch as future work.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the rule-based gate costs about zero tokens, so the saving is nearly all of the avoided slow calls. Not a test of a learned gate.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Value-Guided Search for Efficient Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (arXiv 2505.17373 v2)
finding: Gap 8 partly: a small token-level value model scores partial reasoning blocks and steers the search, with a final weighted vote. It beats majority voting at the same number of generations and cuts length. It is a learned cached-value plug-in used for pruning, not a truncated-reasoning-plus-value answer tested at equal tokens.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, N=256 generations: VGS with 1.5B value model averaged 39.8 on AIME-25 and HMMT-25 (46.7 and 32.8) vs 37.0 for weighted voting with the same scorer and 31.6 for majority voting at 256. Block size 4096 tokens, beam width 2. VGS responses 11,219 tokens vs 12,793 (12% shorter). Value-model compute is 0.024% of generator FLOPs.
limits: Value model trained on 2.5 million traces from the same family; competition math only. The FLOPs saving is shown as a curve to equal accuracy; the exact multiple was not in the text I extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: cheap value estimates on partial thought help at equal generations. No direct 'stop early and use the cached guess' test yet.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring LMs through counterfactual tasks (NAACL 2024; arXiv 2307.02477 v3)
finding: Gap 5: familiar-task shortcuts persist when the task is changed. On 11 counterfactual task pairs (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, rotated drawing, altered chess rules), models are above chance but fall well below the default versions. Closest LLM analogue to a stale cache after devaluation.
numbers: 11 task pairs; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2. Example: parseable programs by GPT-3.5 fall from 99% (default) to 62%, 71% and 75% under three rotation variants. 0-shot chain of thought hurts some default tasks ('overthinking', PaLM-2 base-10 addition, chord fingering).
limits: Exact per-task accuracies are in figures I could not extract. A memorised pattern is not the same as a cached answer from the agent's own earlier solved case.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly: models over-trust default procedures. No study found that tests an agent's own cached solution after the task changed.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs (ICLR 2025; arXiv 2410.05229 v2)
finding: Gap 5: adding one irrelevant clause (GSM-NoOp) to known problem types breaks the learned procedure. Models convert statements to operations by pattern, for example 'discount' becomes multiplication.
numbers: GSM-NoOp accuracy drop: Phi-3-mini over 65%; o1-preview -17.5; Gemma-7b-it -20.6; Mistral-7b-v0.3 -24.0; o1-mini -29.1. Changing only numbers lowers accuracy and raises variance; more clauses lower it further. 8 shots of NoOp examples did not fix it.
limits: Tests robustness of learned patterns, not an agent's own cache. Drops are as read from figure labels.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the fast path (pattern answer) fails silently when a detail changes. The slow check must look for changed conditions, not confidence.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks (arXiv 2302.08399 v5)
finding: Gap 5: a model that looked successful on a famous false-belief task gave the memorised answer when small details broke the pattern (transparent bag, protagonist who can see inside). Einstellung-like failure under a changed task.
numbers: GPT-3.5, transparent-bag variant: 'She believes that the bag is full of chocolate' P(chocolate)=95%, P(popcorn)=0%, although she can see popcorn. Original unexpected-contents task (Kosinski): belief prompt P(chocolate)=99%. A second, unrelated belief prompt did not flip (P(popcorn)=58%).
limits: A few hand-made vignettes; GPT-3.5 only. Anecdotal rather than a benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: supports a rule that pattern or cached answers need a change check, but is not a controlled cache study.
